news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Friday, November 13, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Hantavirus Cases Highlight Climate-Driven Zoonotic Spillover Risks by November 10, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 5 mins read 0 Hantavirus Cases Highlight Climate-Driven Zoonotic Spillover Risks Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Recent reports of hantavirus-associated disease linked to cruise travel in South America have renewed international attention to the growing influence of climate and environmental change on zoonotic disease emergence. Although the World Health Organization currently assesses the public health risk associated with this specific event as low, the outbreak serves as a timely reminder that zoonotic spillover is increasingly shaped by ecological disruption, climate variability, and human mobility. While hantavirus disease remains concentrated in specific endemic regions, the ecological mechanisms underlying its transmission provide valuable insights into how climate and environmental change can influence zoonotic disease risks more broadly. This perspective, published in BMC Global and Public Health, argues that the recent event illustrates a critical shift in global health preparedness, moving from isolated biological events to complex socioecological challenges. The emergence and spread of zoonotic diseases have become defining challenges of the twenty-first century. Approximately 60% of emerging infectious diseases in humans are zoonotic in origin, and most arise from wildlife reservoirs. Historically, disease emergence was often viewed as an isolated biological event. However, growing evidence indicates that climate change, biodiversity loss, land-use change, agricultural expansion, and urbanisation are altering ecological systems in ways that facilitate pathogen transmission between animals and humans. These changes influence wildlife host dynamics, vector ecology, pathogen persistence, and human exposure, creating new opportunities for disease emergence and spread. The recent hantavirus event provides a timely example of this transition, illustrating how ecological disruption and global connectivity can intersect to amplify spillover opportunities and public health concerns. Importantly, such events highlight a critical weakness in current global preparedness systems: surveillance and response frameworks remain overwhelmingly reactive, focusing primarily on outbreak detection after human transmission has already occurred, rather than on anticipating ecological conditions associated with spillover emergence. As climate-related environmental change accelerates globally, understanding the ecological drivers of spillover is becoming increasingly important for global health preparedness. The occurrence of hantavirus cases within ecotourism and international travel networks demonstrates how localised ecological disturbances can be amplified by global mobility, turning a regional health issue into an international concern. This intersection of local ecology and global connectivity underscores the need for a more anticipatory approach to disease surveillance. Discover more Check Symptoms Find Treatments Track Weather Check Forecasts health Hantaviruses are rodent-borne pathogens maintained in wildlife reservoir species, particularly rodents within the Muridae and Cricetidae families. Human infection typically occurs through inhalation of aerosolised particles contaminated with rodent urine, saliva, or feces. Unlike directly transmitted respiratory pathogens, hantaviruses primarily represent environmentally mediated zoonotic spillover events occurring at the human–animal–environment interface. From an eco-epidemiological perspective, hantavirus transmission dynamics are tightly coupled to rodent population ecology. Climatic factors such as rainfall, temperature, humidity, and vegetation productivity strongly influence rodent abundance, breeding cycles, and habitat distribution. This coupling means that shifts in climate directly impact the likelihood of human exposure to the pathogen. Increased rainfall can promote vegetation growth and food availability, leading to rapid rodent population expansion, whereas drought conditions may drive rodents closer to human settlements. Both scenarios can increase opportunities for zoonotic transmission. Extreme weather events, including floods, droughts, and storms, may further alter host–pathogen interactions and increase spillover risk. As climate change intensifies the frequency and severity of such events globally, the ecological systems governing zoonotic spillover are becoming increasingly unstable and unpredictable. Discover more Health Get Health Tips Track Outbreaks These dynamics extend well beyond hantaviruses. Climate-sensitive mechanisms are increasingly recognised across a broad range of infectious diseases. For example, dengue fever continues to expand geographically in response to changing temperature and rainfall patterns, while flooding events contribute to outbreaks of leptospirosis and other environmentally mediated diseases. The emergence of Japanese encephalitis virus in southeastern Australia since 2022 has further highlighted how environmental change, vector ecology, wildlife reservoirs, and animal hosts can converge to facilitate disease emergence. Recent outbreaks of Ebola virus disease in Africa and the COVID-19 pandemic have likewise demonstrated how localised spillover events can rapidly escalate into international public health emergencies. Together, these examples illustrate how environmental change, ecological disruption, and global connectivity are reshaping infectious disease risks across borders. Climate affects not only pathogen survival and vector biology, but also biodiversity, wildlife behaviour, ecosystem stability, and human exposure patterns. Emerging infectious diseases must therefore be understood not solely as biomedical phenomena, but as manifestations of increasingly unstable socioecological systems. At the same time, international travel and trade enable emerging infections to spread rapidly beyond their origins and become regional concerns. The COVID-19 pandemic further reinforced the consequences of failing to address ecological drivers of disease emergence. Although the origins of SARS-CoV-2 remain under investigation, the pandemic demonstrated how ecological disruption, wildlife interfaces, and global mobility can rapidly transform localised spillover events into global public health emergencies. This experience exposed significant limitations in existing preparedness systems, which remained largely reactive, focusing on outbreaks after human cases occur. Yet many zoonotic diseases are preceded by measurable environmental and ecological changes, highlighting the need to strengthen climate-informed surveillance systems capable of identifying elevated spillover risk before outbreaks emerge. The One Health framework provides an important foundation for addressing these challenges. By integrating human, animal, and environmental health surveillance, One Health can improve understanding of disease emergence and support earlier intervention. However, despite widespread policy support, operational implementation remains fragmented across many countries and institutions. The recent hantavirus event highlights the urgent need to strengthen climate-informed and ecologically informed surveillance systems. Future pandemic preparedness must move beyond reactive outbreak response toward anticipatory frameworks capable of identifying spillover risk before sustained human transmission occurs. Recent advances in remote sensing, artificial intelligence, environmental monitoring, climate forecasting, and predictive analytics provide new opportunities to operationalise this approach. Environmental indicators, including rainfall anomalies, vegetation change, temperature variability, and land-use patterns, may help identify ecological conditions associated with increased disease risk before widespread transmission occurs. An important future direction will be the development of integrated climate-informed early warning systems capable of linking environmental monitoring, ecological surveillance, wildlife reservoir dynamics, and human disease data in near real time. Such systems may help identify ecological conditions associated with elevated spillover risk, support spatial risk prediction, and enable earlier public health intervention before widespread transmission occurs. A conceptual framework for these systems outlines the integration of diverse data streams to create a cohesive early warning capability. Integrating climate, environmental, wildlife, vector, and human disease surveillance data within a One Health framework may improve early detection of zoonotic spillover risk. Such systems can support risk prediction, hotspot detection, early warning, and public health preparedness for climate-sensitive emerging infectious diseases. More broadly, climate change is no longer simply a contextual background factor for infectious diseases. Rather, it is increasingly reshaping the ecological systems governing reservoir host dynamics, vector ecology, pathogen maintenance, and human exposure patterns. As biodiversity loss, land-use change, and environmental disruption continue to intensify globally, the frequency and complexity of zoonotic spillover events are likely to increase. These challenges expose important limitations in predominantly reactive outbreak-response systems. Future preparedness will require more anticipatory and integrated approaches capable of linking climate science, environmental monitoring, wildlife surveillance, and public health systems within climate-informed One Health frameworks. Advances in remote sensing, predictive modelling, and environmental intelligence may provide important opportunities to strengthen early warning capacity and improve preparedness for climate-sensitive emerging infectious diseases. Ultimately, the recent hantavirus event should not be interpreted as an isolated outbreak, but as part of a broader planetary health challenge emerging from increasingly unstable interactions among climate, ecosystems, wildlife, and human societies. Strengthening climate-informed One Health approaches may therefore become one of the most important priorities for reducing future pandemic risk in a rapidly changing environmental future. Subject of Research: The impact of climate change and ecological disruption on zoonotic spillover dynamics and the need for climate-informed One Health surveillance systems. Both scenarios can increase opportunities for zoonotic transmission. Extreme weather events, including floods, droughts, and storms, may further alter host–pathogen interactions and increase spillover risk. As climate change intensifies the frequency and severity of such events globally, the ecological systems governing zoonotic spillover are becoming increasingly unstable and unpredictable. Discover more Health Get Health Tips Track Outbreaks These dynamics extend well beyond hantaviruses. Climate-sensitive mechanisms are increasingly recognised across a broad range of infectious diseases. For example, dengue fever continues to expand geographically in response to changing temperature and rainfall patterns, while flooding events contribute to outbreaks of leptospirosis and other environmentally mediated diseases. The emergence of Japanese encephalitis virus in southeastern Australia since 2022 has further highlighted how environmental change, vector ecology, wildlife reservoirs, and animal hosts can converge to facilitate disease emergence. Recent outbreaks of Ebola virus disease in Africa and the COVID-19 pandemic have likewise demonstrated how localised spillover events can rapidly escalate into international public health emergencies. Together, these examples illustrate how environmental change, ecological disruption, and global connectivity are reshaping infectious disease risks across borders. Climate affects not only pathogen survival and vector biology, but also biodiversity, wildlife behaviour, ecosystem stability, and human exposure patterns. Emerging infectious diseases must therefore be understood not solely as biomedical phenomena, but as manifestations of increasingly unstable socioecological systems. At the same time, international travel and trade enable emerging infections to spread rapidly beyond their origins and become regional concerns. The COVID-19 pandemic further reinforced the consequences of failing to address ecological drivers of disease emergence. Although the origins of SARS-CoV-2 remain under investigation, the pandemic demonstrated how ecological disruption, wildlife interfaces, and global mobility can rapidly transform localised spillover events into global public health emergencies. This experience exposed significant limitations in existing preparedness systems, which remained largely reactive, focusing on outbreaks after human cases occur. Yet many zoonotic diseases are preceded by measurable environmental and ecological changes, highlighting the need to strengthen climate-informed surveillance systems capable of identifying elevated spillover risk before outbreaks emerge. The One Health framework provides an important foundation for addressing these challenges. By integrating human, animal, and environmental health surveillance, One Health can improve understanding of disease emergence and support earlier intervention. However, despite widespread policy support, operational implementation remains fragmented across many countries and institutions. The recent hantavirus event highlights the urgent need to strengthen climate-informed and ecologically informed surveillance systems. Future pandemic preparedness must move beyond reactive outbreak response toward anticipatory frameworks capable of identifying spillover risk before sustained human transmission occurs. Recent advances in remote sensing, artificial intelligence, environmental monitoring, climate forecasting, and predictive analytics provide new opportunities to operationalise this approach. Environmental indicators, including rainfall anomalies, vegetation change, temperature variability, and land-use patterns, may help identify ecological conditions associated with increased disease risk before widespread transmission occurs. An important future direction will be the development of integrated climate-informed early warning systems capable of linking environmental monitoring, ecological surveillance, wildlife reservoir dynamics, and human disease data in near real time. Such systems may help identify ecological conditions associated with elevated spillover risk, support spatial risk prediction, and enable earlier public health intervention before widespread transmission occurs. A conceptual framework for these systems outlines the integration of diverse data streams to create a cohesive early warning capability. Integrating climate, environmental, wildlife, vector, and human disease surveillance data within a One Health framework may improve early detection of zoonotic spillover risk. Such systems can support risk prediction, hotspot detection, early warning, and public health preparedness for climate-sensitive emerging infectious diseases. More broadly, climate change is no longer simply a contextual background factor for infectious diseases. Rather, it is increasingly reshaping the ecological systems governing reservoir host dynamics, vector ecology, pathogen maintenance, and human exposure patterns. As biodiversity loss, land-use change, and environmental disruption continue to intensify globally, the frequency and complexity of zoonotic spillover events are likely to increase. These challenges expose important limitations in predominantly reactive outbreak-response systems. Future preparedness will require more anticipatory and integrated approaches capable of linking climate science, environmental monitoring, wildlife surveillance, and public health systems within climate-informed One Health frameworks. Advances in remote sensing, predictive modelling, and environmental intelligence may provide important opportunities to strengthen early warning capacity and improve preparedness for climate-sensitive emerging infectious diseases. Ultimately, the recent hantavirus event should not be interpreted as an isolated outbreak, but as part of a broader planetary health challenge emerging from increasingly unstable interactions among climate, ecosystems, wildlife, and human societies. Strengthening climate-informed One Health approaches may therefore become one of the most important priorities for reducing future pandemic risk in a rapidly changing environmental future. news.content: A Spanish passenger, disembarked from the MV Hondius cruise ship and infected with hantavirus, before boarding a plane from Tenerife, Spain, on May 10, 2026. AP Several months after the official end of the hantavirus outbreak, declared on July 2 by the World Health Organization (WHO), an international consortium of experts analyzed the genomic sequences of 10 patients infected by this virus originating from South America. This study , published on Thursday, November 12, in the journal Science , confirms most of the epidemiological hypotheses put forward so far and opens up new avenues for research. The study also demonstrates, if further proof were needed, the necessity of working together on an international scale to avoid misinterpretation. To understand what is at stake with such work, it is important to recall how this family of viruses – unknown to the public and even most experts – suddenly alarmed the scientific community, only to be almost forgotten 42 days later, once the quarantines of roughly 650 close contacts ended without any new infections. The alert was raised on May 2: Three passengers from the exploratory cruise ship MV Hondius had already died from a respiratory infection; a hantavirus was detected in one of them. The culprit was formally identified three days later in South Africa: It was the Andes strain, the only hantavirus known to be transmissible between humans, previously observed only in Argentina and Chile. In total, 13 people were infected, resulting in a fatality rate of 23%. You have 83.67% of this article left to read. The rest is for subscribers only

news.title: No Hantavirus Spread Found After Cruise. Off-Ship Risk Likely 2% Or Less
news.excerpt: CDC followed 88 U.S. residents after the MV Hondius hantavirus outbreak and identified no secondary infections. Global counts bound the risk to contacts.
news.rss_summary_html: CDC followed 88 U.S. residents after the MV Hondius hantavirus outbreak and identified no secondary infections. Global counts bound the risk to contacts.
news.priority_tier_reason: 可信机构来源或已成功抓获正文
news.content_title: No Hantavirus Spread Found After Cruise. Off-Ship Risk Likely 2% Or Less
news.content: ROTTERDAM, NETHERLANDS - MAY 18: Specialist workers in full PPE onboard the cruise ship MV Hondius after it docked in the Port of Rotterdam to be disinfected following the recent hantavirus outbreak, on May 18, 2026 in Rotterdam, Netherlands. The cruise ship MV Hondius is docking in Rotterdam where crew members will be tested and quarantined and the ship will be disinfected after three passengers aboard the nature cruise died from Hantavirus over recent weeks. On May 10, the remaining passengers docked in Tenerife, in Spain's Canary Islands, where they were repatriated to their respective countries to be monitored, and in some cases, quarantined. As of May 15, a total of 10 cases have been confirmed by the World Health Organization, including the three who died from the disease, which can be contracted through contact with the urine, feces, or saliva of infected rodents. (Photo by Omar Havana/Getty Images) Hantavirus does not appear to have spread beyond the cruise ship MV Hondius last spring. By my estimate the risk to contacts who never sailed was no more than 2 percent. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has reported that it identified no secondary infections among 88 U.S. residents followed for 42 days, 28 of whom had sailed. Worldwide, about 653 contacts from 33 countries were monitored. The outbreak ended with 13 cases and three deaths , all among people who had been aboard. The cause, Andes virus, is the only hantavirus known to spread between people . In May I argued that it would not be the next pandemic . Clearly, it was not. No infections were found among about 480 contacts who never sailed, which puts their risk below about 0.6 percent, with 95 percent confidence. For the roughly 150 of them with high-risk exposure, the upper bound is about 2 percent. Risk was far higher for those who sailed: 10 of 121 passengers and 3 of 61 crew members became cases, about 7 percent overall, including at least one person probably infected before boarding. Closeness raises risk. In a study of households in Chile , 17.6 percent of patients' sex partners developed the disease, compared with 1.2 percent of other household contacts. A risk of 2 percent or less is small and may not be zero, which fits what both the U.S. CDC and the World Health Organization have said, although they interpreted it differently. For WHO the follow-up "demonstrates effective interruption of transmission." In contrast, the CDC cautioned that the absence of infections among U.S. contacts "should not be interpreted as evidence that no transmission risk existed." Neither is wrong. I calculated those upper bounds with a statistical shortcut called the rule of three . It is an interesting (and useful!) mathematical fact. When an event has not occurred in a group, we can be about 95 percent confident that its true rate is below three divided by the group's size. (The calculation assumes that each person's outcome is independent of everyone else's and that everyone has the same risk.) WHO listed 317 high-risk and 336 low-risk contacts, but those figures include people from the ship, and anyone aboard found to be infected was counted as a case. Removing from the high-risk list the 169 people who sailed and were not counted as cases leaves about 150 who never sailed, assuming all 169 were on the list. Taking the same 169 from the 653 total leaves about 480. The true upper bounds may be slightly higher. The estimate counts only infections that were detected, largely through symptoms, and Andes virus can cause mild illness . Contacts were monitored and many were quarantined, so the figures describe risk under those precautions. Additionally, exposure varied widely: of the 60 U.S. flight contacts, 57 were on a plane that a sick cruise passenger, in the CDC's words, "briefly boarded then disembarked." The cruise ship MV Hondius is docking in Rotterdam where crew members will be tested and quarantined and the ship will be disinfected after three passengers aboard the nature cruise died from Hantavirus over recent weeks. On May 10, the remaining passengers docked in Tenerife, in Spain's Canary Islands, where they were repatriated to their respective countries to be monitored, and in some cases, quarantined. As of May 15, a total of 10 cases have been confirmed by the World Health Organization, including the three who died from the disease, which can be contracted through contact with the urine, feces, or saliva of infected rodents. By my estimate the risk to contacts who never sailed was no more than 2 percent. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has reported that it identified no secondary infections among 88 U.S. residents followed for 42 days, 28 of whom had sailed. Worldwide, about 653 contacts from 33 countries were monitored. The outbreak ended with 13 cases and three deaths , all among people who had been aboard. The cause, Andes virus, is the only hantavirus known to spread between people . In May I argued that it would not be the next pandemic . Clearly, it was not. No infections were found among about 480 contacts who never sailed, which puts their risk below about 0.6 percent, with 95 percent confidence. For the roughly 150 of them with high-risk exposure, the upper bound is about 2 percent. Risk was far higher for those who sailed: 10 of 121 passengers and 3 of 61 crew members became cases, about 7 percent overall, including at least one person probably infected before boarding. Closeness raises risk. In a study of households in Chile , 17.6 percent of patients' sex partners developed the disease, compared with 1.2 percent of other household contacts. A risk of 2 percent or less is small and may not be zero, which fits what both the U.S. CDC and the World Health Organization have said, although they interpreted it differently. For WHO the follow-up "demonstrates effective interruption of transmission." In contrast, the CDC cautioned that the absence of infections among U.S. contacts "should not be interpreted as evidence that no transmission risk existed." Neither is wrong. I calculated those upper bounds with a statistical shortcut called the rule of three . It is an interesting (and useful!) mathematical fact. When an event has not occurred in a group, we can be about 95 percent confident that its true rate is below three divided by the group's size. (The calculation assumes that each person's outcome is independent of everyone else's and that everyone has the same risk.) WHO listed 317 high-risk and 336 low-risk contacts, but those figures include people from the ship, and anyone aboard found to be infected was counted as a case. Removing from the high-risk list the 169 people who sailed and were not counted as cases leaves about 150 who never sailed, assuming all 169 were on the list. Taking the same 169 from the 653 total leaves about 480. The true upper bounds may be slightly higher. The estimate counts only infections that were detected, largely through symptoms, and Andes virus can cause mild illness . Contacts were monitored and many were quarantined, so the figures describe risk under those precautions. Additionally, exposure varied widely: of the 60 U.S. flight contacts, 57 were on a plane that a sick cruise passenger, in the CDC's words, "briefly boarded then disembarked." Contacts on one plane also share a single exposure, which raises the upper bounds. Nonetheless, it is safe to conclude that the risk of transmission outside the close quarters of the cruise ship was small. There was never any chance of a pandemic. Now, a study published in the journal “Science” provides new insights into the matter. Redaktion blue News, Keystone-SDA 12.11.2026, 20:00•12.11.2026, 22:34 Here's what it's all about In the spring of 2026, a total of 13 people on the "Hondius" contracted the Andes virus, and three people died. A new study published in the journal *Science* now provides clues as to the origin of the pathogen. However, the original source of the infection remains unclear. Summary created with The cruise ship “Hondius” made headlines around the world in the spring of 2026: An outbreak of the Hantavirus on the ship claimed the lives of three people. On Thursday, the journal “Science” published a study with new findings on the spread of the disease. It remains unclear, however, where the passengers originally became infected. The study does show, however, that the virus is closely related to a variant that has been circulating for years in a limited region in northern Patagonia. Researchers from the University of Geneva and the Geneva University Hospitals (HUG) also participated in the study. In April 2026, an unprecedented outbreak of the hantavirus occurred on the Dutch-flagged “Hondius.” A total of 13 passengers were infected, and three people died. Among those affected was a person residing in Switzerland. The origin of the virus remains a mystery The research team compared the virus's genetic sequences with older samples from South America. This revealed a close genetic relationship with viruses that had been detected during an outbreak in Villa Meliquina, in the Argentine province of Neuquén, in 2018. Epidemiologists identified a couple who had spent months traveling through Chile and Argentina in a motorhome before the cruise as the source of the chain of infection. Using border crossing records and other information, the researchers reconstructed the couple's travel route. In doing so, they did find that they had stayed in the known endemic region in Patagonia. However, these events occurred too far before the onset of the illness to be consistent with the virus’s incubation period. A documented stay in Neuquén Province took place approximately 62 days before the first symptoms appeared. According to the study, however, the incubation period for the Andes virus is no more than 40 days. Stowaways in a RV? The researchers therefore suspect alternative scenarios: Either there was a previously undetected intermediate infection via a third person (human-to-human), or rodents infected with the virus, such as the long-tailed dwarf rice rat, traveled as “stowaways” in the couple’s RV for an extended period before the infection occurred—or the RV was contaminated in some other way. According to the study’s authors, the incident highlights a new reality in global health: The outbreak shows that viruses previously considered geographically limited can appear in unexpected locations through infected people, the researchers write. “This calls into question previous assumptions about the geographic predictability of future outbreaks,” the researchers write in the study. OffOn Stream on Officials in Arizona, Georgia monitoring some hantavirus cruise ship passengers who have returned to US None of the residents being monitored in the U.S. have shown signs of illness. ByZoe Magee, Dragana Jovanovic, and Mary Kekatos May 7, 2026, 3:13 AM Share The total number of confirmed hantavirus cases aboard a cruise ship has risen to five as global health authorities work to contain a potentially deadly cluster of the disease. More than 100 passengers remain on the ship, MV Hondius, and the World Health Organization (WHO) is monitoring their health. Officials said that the "overall public health risk remains low" but that there may be some person-to-person spread. In its first public statement on the outbreak on Wednesday evening, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said, "the risk to the American public is extremely low" and urged Americans aboard the ship to follow the guidance of health officials. "Our top priority remains the health and safety of all U.S. passengers," the CDC statement said. "The Department of State is leading a coordinated, whole-of-government response including direct contact with passengers, diplomatic coordination, and engagement with domestic and international health authorities." Officials in Arizona, Georgia monitoring passengers who have returned to US Health officials in multiple states in the U.S. say they are monitoring some passengers who have returned to the U.S. after being aboard the ship for potential hantavirus infections. The Arizona Department of Health Services said it is monitoring one resident that was a passenger on the ship. The Georgia Department of Public Health said it is monitoring two residents who returned home after disembarking from the Hondius. None of the former passengers being monitored in the U.S. have shown any signs of illness, officials said. Cape Verdean police officers stand guard as crew members of an ambulance boat getting in hazmat suites preparing to head to the cruise ship MV Hondius, while stationary off the port of Praia, the capital of Cape Verde, on May 6, 2026. AFP via Getty Images Ship's route The ship, which was off the coast of Africa in Cape Verde, is now en route to the Canary Islands after officials medically evacuated three people, including two in "serious condition." The trip is expected to take three to four days, the ship's operator, Oceanwide Expeditions, said Wednesday. Some passengers disembarked the ship before knowledge of the cluster and are back in their home countries. In some cases, authorities are advising those passengers to self-isolate. The two patients who were evacuated have landed in the Netherlands and "have been received by specialist medical and screening teams," Oceanwide Expeditions said Wednesday. In addition to those two, a third person, who is asymptomatic but a close contact of a German national who died on May 2, was also removed from the ship, WHO officials in Cape Verde told ABC News. The medical aircraft transporting the individual is experiencing a delay, Oceanwide Expeditions said Wednesday. "WHO continues to work with the ship’s operators to closely monitor the health of passengers and crew, working with countries to support appropriate medical follow-up and evacuation where needed," Dr. Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, the director-general of the WHO, said in a post on X on Wednesday, in which he confirmed the evacuations. "Monitoring and follow-up for passengers on board and for those who have already disembarked has been initiated in collaboration with the ship's operators and national health authorities," he continued. Tedros added that "the overall public health risk remains low." For now, there are no symptomatic passengers who remain on board the ship, Dr. Freddy Banza, a WHO doctor who helped evacuate the three people, told reporters Wednesday. The people now considered at highest risk are the crew members and medical staff who spent the most time caring for sick passengers, he said. Related 3 people waiting to be medically evacuated from cruise ship at center of suspected hantavirus outbreak Health officials confirmed two additional cases of hantavirus among crewmembers, bringing the total confirmed cases to five. Popular Reads Baby buried alive for 24 hours released from the hospital; father charged 1 day ago 8 dead, including 2 children, after building collapses in Brooklyn 1 hour ago Wisconsin state trooper detained by ICE Nov 6 "Swiss authorities have confirmed a case of hantavirus identified in a passenger from the MV Hondius cruise ship," the WHO said on X on Wednesday. "He had responded to an email from the ship’s operator informing the passengers of the health event, and presented himself to a hospital in Zurich, Switzerland, and is receiving care." 3 deaths recorded The three previously confirmed hantavirus cases include a woman who disembarked and was on her way home from the Netherlands, a British national who is in critical but stable condition in a hospital in Johannesburg, and a passenger who traveled on the first leg of the voyage and is currently being treated at the University Hospital Zurich, according to Oceanwide Expeditions. So far, three deaths have been recorded. In a statement, the Dutch airline KLM said it had been informed by Dutch health authorities that one of the people who died from the hantavirus was briefly aboard a KLM aircraft in Johannesburg, South Africa, on April 25. "Due to the passenger’s medical condition at the time, the crew decided not to allow the passenger to travel on the flight," the airline said in the statement. "The passenger sadly later passed away in Johannesburg." The airline said all passengers who were on board the flight were being notified. The type of virus in this outbreak has been confirmed as Andes hantavirus by the National Institute for Communicable Diseases in South Africa and Geneva University Hospitals in Switzerland, the WHO said Wednesday. The Andes hantavirus historically has been shown to potentially transmit between people, according to the WHO. Oceanwide Expeditions said of the three passengers who were evacuated from the ship, two are symptomatic and in serious condition and the third is asymptomatic but a close contact of a German national who died on May 2. This aerial view shows crew members wearing hazmat suits on board of a boat heading towards the port from the cruise ship MV Hondius, stationary off the port of Praia, the capital of Cape Verde, on May 6, 2026. AFP via Getty Images "In partnership with the RIVM (Dutch Institute for Public Health and Environment), Oceanwide Expeditions is expanding medical care on board with two infectious disease physicians, arriving today by plane from the Netherlands. This ensures that optimal medical care can be provided if necessary, during the next stage of this evolving situation," the company said in a statement. Cape Verde officials said on Tuesday that the vessel was expected to sail to the Spanish island of Tenerife, but the president of the Canary Islands, a Spanish archipelago off the northwestern coast of Africa, said on Wednesday that the regional government was opposed to allowing the luxury cruise ship to dock in Tenerife. "This decision is not based on any technical criteria, nor is there sufficient information to reassure the public or guarantee their safety," President Fernando Clavijo told radio station COPE, according to Reuters. Related American speaks out from cruise ship amid deadly hantavirus outbreak Clavijo said on social media that he had requested a meeting with the Spanish prime minister to discuss the ship. He added that the Canary Islands "always acts with responsibility, but it cannot accept decisions taken behind the backs of the Canary Islands institutions and without sufficient information to the population." Mónica García, Spain's minister of health, said once the ship arrives at the port of Granadilla de Abona in the Canary Islands, there will be a "joint screening and evacuation mechanism will be launched to repatriate all passengers," according to RTVE, a Spanish national public broadcaster. A general view of the cruise ship MV Hondius, while stationary off the port of Praia, the capital of Cape Verde, on May 6, 2026. AFP via Getty Images “Unless their medical condition prevents it, all foreign passengers will be repatriated through the European civil protection mechanism, about which the Interior Minister will provide further details later," Garcia said in Spanish. WHO officials earlier on Wednesday said the three evacuated people were to be transferred to planes bound for both the Netherlands and Tenerife, but later updated the plan so that all would be sent to the Netherlands, officials told ABC News. ABC News' Othon Leyva contributed to this report. OffOn Stream on Officials in Arizona, Georgia monitoring some hantavirus cruise ship passengers who have returned to US None of the residents being monitored in the U.S. have shown signs of illness. ByZoe Magee, Dragana Jovanovic, and Mary Kekatos May 7, 2026, 3:13 AM Share The total number of confirmed hantavirus cases aboard a cruise ship has risen to five as global health authorities work to contain a potentially deadly cluster of the disease. More than 100 passengers remain on the ship, MV Hondius, and the World Health Organization (WHO) is monitoring their health. Officials said that the "overall public health risk remains low" but that there may be some person-to-person spread. In its first public statement on the outbreak on Wednesday evening, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said, "the risk to the American public is extremely low" and urged Americans aboard the ship to follow the guidance of health officials. "Our top priority remains the health and safety of all U.S. passengers," the CDC statement said. "The Department of State is leading a coordinated, whole-of-government response including direct contact with passengers, diplomatic coordination, and engagement with domestic and international health authorities." Officials in Arizona, Georgia monitoring passengers who have returned to US Health officials in multiple states in the U.S. say they are monitoring some passengers who have returned to the U.S. after being aboard the ship for potential hantavirus infections. The Arizona Department of Health Services said it is monitoring one resident that was a passenger on the ship. The Georgia Department of Public Health said it is monitoring two residents who returned home after disembarking from the Hondius. None of the former passengers being monitored in the U.S. have shown any signs of illness, officials said. Cape Verdean police officers stand guard as crew members of an ambulance boat getting in hazmat suites preparing to head to the cruise ship MV Hondius, while stationary off the port of Praia, the capital of Cape Verde, on May 6, 2026. AFP via Getty Images Ship's route The ship, which was off the coast of Africa in Cape Verde, is now en route to the Canary Islands after officials medically evacuated three people, including two in "serious condition." The trip is expected to take three to four days, the ship's operator, Oceanwide Expeditions, said Wednesday. Some passengers disembarked the ship before knowledge of the cluster and are back in their home countries. In some cases, authorities are advising those passengers to self-isolate. The two patients who were evacuated have landed in the Netherlands and "have been received by specialist medical and screening teams," Oceanwide Expeditions said Wednesday. In addition to those two, a third person, who is asymptomatic but a close contact of a German national who died on May 2, was also removed from the ship, WHO officials in Cape Verde told ABC News. The medical aircraft transporting the individual is experiencing a delay, Oceanwide Expeditions said Wednesday. "WHO continues to work with the ship’s operators to closely monitor the health of passengers and crew, working with countries to support appropriate medical follow-up and evacuation where needed," Dr. Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, the director-general of the WHO, said in a post on X on Wednesday, in which he confirmed the evacuations. "Monitoring and follow-up for passengers on board and for those who have already disembarked has been initiated in collaboration with the ship's operators and national health authorities," he continued. Tedros added that "the overall public health risk remains low." For now, there are no symptomatic passengers who remain on board the ship, Dr. Freddy Banza, a WHO doctor who helped evacuate the three people, told reporters Wednesday. The people now considered at highest risk are the crew members and medical staff who spent the most time caring for sick passengers, he said. Related 3 people waiting to be medically evacuated from cruise ship at center of suspected hantavirus outbreak Health officials confirmed two additional cases of hantavirus among crewmembers, bringing the total confirmed cases to five. Popular Reads Baby buried alive for 24 hours released from the hospital; father charged 1 day ago 8 dead, including 2 children, after building collapses in Brooklyn 1 hour ago Wisconsin state trooper detained by ICE Nov 6 "Swiss authorities have confirmed a case of hantavirus identified in a passenger from the MV Hondius cruise ship," the WHO said on X on Wednesday. "He had responded to an email from the ship’s operator informing the passengers of the health event, and presented himself to a hospital in Zurich, Switzerland, and is receiving care." 3 deaths recorded The three previously confirmed hantavirus cases include a woman who disembarked and was on her way home from the Netherlands, a British national who is in critical but stable condition in a hospital in Johannesburg, and a passenger who traveled on the first leg of the voyage and is currently being treated at the University Hospital Zurich, according to Oceanwide Expeditions. So far, three deaths have been recorded. In a statement, the Dutch airline KLM said it had been informed by Dutch health authorities that one of the people who died from the hantavirus was briefly aboard a KLM aircraft in Johannesburg, South Africa, on April 25. "Due to the passenger’s medical condition at the time, the crew decided not to allow the passenger to travel on the flight," the airline said in the statement. "The passenger sadly later passed away in Johannesburg." The airline said all passengers who were on board the flight were being notified. The type of virus in this outbreak has been confirmed as Andes hantavirus by the National Institute for Communicable Diseases in South Africa and Geneva University Hospitals in Switzerland, the WHO said Wednesday. The Andes hantavirus historically has been shown to potentially transmit between people, according to the WHO. Oceanwide Expeditions said of the three passengers who were evacuated from the ship, two are symptomatic and in serious condition and the third is asymptomatic but a close contact of a German national who died on May 2. This aerial view shows crew members wearing hazmat suits on board of a boat heading towards the port from the cruise ship MV Hondius, stationary off the port of Praia, the capital of Cape Verde, on May 6, 2026. AFP via Getty Images "In partnership with the RIVM (Dutch Institute for Public Health and Environment), Oceanwide Expeditions is expanding medical care on board with two infectious disease physicians, arriving today by plane from the Netherlands. This ensures that optimal medical care can be provided if necessary, during the next stage of this evolving situation," the company said in a statement. Cape Verde officials said on Tuesday that the vessel was expected to sail to the Spanish island of Tenerife, but the president of the Canary Islands, a Spanish archipelago off the northwestern coast of Africa, said on Wednesday that the regional government was opposed to allowing the luxury cruise ship to dock in Tenerife. "This decision is not based on any technical criteria, nor is there sufficient information to reassure the public or guarantee their safety," President Fernando Clavijo told radio station COPE, according to Reuters. Related American speaks out from cruise ship amid deadly hantavirus outbreak Clavijo said on social media that he had requested a meeting with the Spanish prime minister to discuss the ship. He added that the Canary Islands "always acts with responsibility, but it cannot accept decisions taken behind the backs of the Canary Islands institutions and without sufficient information to the population." Mónica García, Spain's minister of health, said once the ship arrives at the port of Granadilla de Abona in the Canary Islands, there will be a "joint screening and evacuation mechanism will be launched to repatriate all passengers," according to RTVE, a Spanish national public broadcaster. A general view of the cruise ship MV Hondius, while stationary off the port of Praia, the capital of Cape Verde, on May 6, 2026. AFP via Getty Images “Unless their medical condition prevents it, all foreign passengers will be repatriated through the European civil protection mechanism, about which the Interior Minister will provide further details later," Garcia said in Spanish. WHO officials earlier on Wednesday said the three evacuated people were to be transferred to planes bound for both the Netherlands and Tenerife, but later updated the plan so that all would be sent to the Netherlands, officials told ABC News. ABC News' Othon Leyva contributed to this report. OffOn Stream on News Can I get hantavirus from my pet? Here's what pet owners should know Global race to contain hantavirus outbreak ByDr. Geraldine Nabeta May 14, 2026, 10:25 PM The recent headlines about illnesses and deaths tied to possible hantavirus exposure have left some pet owners wondering whether the virus can be spread through the furry creature sleeping on their couch or curled up on their lap. While cats and dogs can be infected with the hantavirus, they generally don’t have symptoms and experts say they are highly unlikely to infect their owners. Related Passenger from hantavirus-stricken cruise ship speaks out from quarantine "They can be exposed, but they don't get sick the way that we know people to get sick," Dr. Kate Elden, the chief medical officer of the veterinary telehealth company, Dutch, told ABC News. "There's no actual test that a veterinarian or your local vet is going to have." And even when a dog or cat does have a hantavirus infection, they don’t transfer the virus to humans, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. However, if they bring an infected wild rodent into the home that could theoretically increase your exposure, Elden cautioned. Stock photo of a dog and cat being fed. Simpleimages/STOCK PHOTO/Getty Images "Don't hesitate to call your vet if your pet brought a rodent home and starts to [look] unwell," she said. Elden advised disposing of any rodent your pet has brought home while wearing a mask and gloves, and then thoroughly washing hands with soap and water after it has safely been dispatched. Even owners of pet rats and mice don’t have much to worry about, Elden said. "The domestic hamster, guinea pig, gerbil, these are captive bred animals, we have no documentation that they play a role in hantavirus cases or are part of spreading the disease," Elden said. To be safe, clean cages away from food preparation and spray down bedding to minimize dust particles in the air if necessary, she advised. Popular Reads Baby buried alive for 24 hours released from the hospital; father charged 1 day ago 8 dead, including 2 children, after building collapses in Brooklyn 1 hour ago Wisconsin state trooper detained by ICE Nov 6 Deer mice are the most likely natural hosts for hantavirus, the CDC notes. Related American who survived hantavirus in 1993 outbreak describes her symptoms and recovery The virus lives in their bodies without making them sick, and they spread it through their urine, droppings and saliva, according to the American Veterinary Medical Association. But your risk depends a lot on where you live. Hantavirus remain rare and scattered in the U.S., according to the CDC, with most cases reported in California, Colorado, New Mexico and Arizona. People typically become infected after inhaling contaminated particles, usually while cleaning sheds, cabins, garages or rodent-infested areas or while doing outdoor activities like hunting and camping. One rare exception is the Andes virus, a strain found mainly in South America that can spread from person to person through close contact and has been linked to the recent cruise ship cases. Pets are not known to spread Andes virus to humans. The CDC lists early symptoms of hantavirus similar to those resembling the flu, including fever, muscle aches, fatigue, headache, nausea and shortness of breath. The infection can quickly take a turn, becoming more severe and affecting the lungs. Related Former White House COVID-19 response coordinator answers hantavirus questions The best way to avoid infection is by reducing rodent activity near your home, Elden said. Seal any holes and clean rodent droppings with a disinfectant instead of sweeping or vacuuming. Keep pet food sealed. And if you think you've been exposed through any source, the CDC recommends seeking immediate medical attention. Geraldine Nabeta MD MSc is an incoming chief resident in internal medicine at the University of Connecticut and a member of the ABC News Medical Unit. supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Friday, November 13, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Hantavirus Neutralizing Antibodies Differ Between Historical Vaccine and Circulating Chinese Strains by November 11, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 4 mins read 0 Hantavirus Neutralizing Antibodies Differ Between Historical Vaccine and Circulating Chinese Strains Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Neutralizing antibody titers against Hantavirus differ significantly between historical vaccine strains and representative circulating epidemic strains in China, according to a comparative evaluation of convalescent patient and vaccinee sera. The investigation assessed whether viral divergence across rodent reservoirs influences the humoral immunity elicited by long-standing immunization programs. Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), caused by Hantavirus, continues to present a significant public health burden globally. In key endemic provinces throughout China, prevention efforts have relied on a bivalent inactivated vaccine formulated with Hantaan virus (HTNV) and Seoul virus (SEOV) strains originally isolated two decades ago. Following decades of comprehensive control measures, HFRS incidence in China has transitioned into a phase of low-level epidemic fluctuation. Nevertheless, ongoing viral transmission within wild rodent host populations can spur dynamic shifts in genetic diversity and immunogenicity, creating uncertainty regarding ongoing vaccine-induced protection and underlying pathogenic mechanisms. To evaluate these immune responses, researchers established a serum panel comprising convalescent samples from clinical HFRS cases alongside specimens from individuals who received standardized immunization with the bivalent inactivated vaccine. Using an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay-based microneutralization test (MN-ELISA), neutralizing antibody titers were measured against the HTNV vaccine strain 84FLi, the SEOV vaccine strain L99, and three representative epidemic strains representing distinct genotypes: HTNV strain SX26 and SEOV strains LN03 and FJ-17. Hantavirus-neutralizing antibodies were successfully detected across all tested serum samples. Among the 48 evaluated HFRS patients, laboratory identification categorized 47.92 percent (23 of 48) as HTNV infections, 27.08 percent (13 of 48) as SEOV infections, and 25 percent (12 of 48) as untypable cases. Titers against vaccine strains and circulating epidemic strains exhibited pronounced divergence. For HTNV, both convalescent patient sera and vaccinee sera demonstrated significantly higher geometric mean titers against the vaccine strain 84FLi compared to the epidemic strain SX26, registering 1:386.08 versus 1:223.04 (P < 0.001) in patients and 1:137.94 versus 1:110.37 (P < 0.05) in vaccinees. In contrast, the pattern reversed for SEOV strains. Patient sera displayed significantly lower geometric mean titers against the L99 vaccine strain than against the epidemic strain LN03, at 1:177.02 versus 1:297.71 (P < 0.01). Similarly, vaccinee sera showed significantly lower titers against L99 compared to the epidemic strain FJ-17, measuring 1:97.52 versus 1:243.71 (P < 0.001), while significant immunogenicity heterogeneity was also observed between the LN03 and FJ-17 epidemic strains. The study authors concluded that Hantavirus genetic diversity and immunogenicity exhibit defined geographical characteristics. Although the current bivalent vaccine stimulates broad neutralizing antibodies and infection confers cross-reactive responses across genotypes, variations in neutralizing efficacy against circulating strains highlight the necessity of continuous regional genomic surveillance and routine evaluation of vaccine matching. The study provides critical nuance regarding how cross-neutralization functions across divergent viral genotypes. While the bivalent inactivated vaccine used in China induces broad neutralizing antibodies, its cross-protective efficacy can vary when challenged by different circulating strains and genotypes. Natural infection with Hantavirus similarly generates cross-neutralizing antibodies whose titers differ significantly depending on the genotype involved, yet still succeed in conferring sufficient cross-protection. Furthermore, the significant immunogenicity heterogeneity identified between the two Seoul virus epidemic strains, LN03 and FJ-17, demonstrates that circulating field isolates from the same virus species can exhibit disparate antigenic properties compared to the historical L99 vaccine strain isolated two decades ago. These shifting antigenic profiles are deeply connected to the natural reservoir dynamics of the pathogen. Although decades of comprehensive prevention and control measures have successfully brought hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome to a stage of low-level epidemic fluctuation in China, continuous viral transmission among rodent host animals persists. This sustained animal-reservoir circulation can drive dynamic changes in the genetic diversity and immunogenicity of Hantavirus. In turn, such shifts have the potential to influence viral pathogenic mechanisms and diminish the protective effectiveness of established vaccines, making timely monitoring and evaluation of viral immunogenicity an indispensable priority. To sustain epidemic control, the study underscores several critical surveillance and public health priorities. The authors highlight the great significance of strengthening surveillance of the genetic characteristics of regional-specific circulating viral strains. In parallel, public health programs must regularly evaluate the matching degree between vaccine protective effectiveness and currently circulating epidemic strains. These coordinated efforts are necessary to predict and evaluate the transmission and pathogenic risks posed by evolving Hantavirus strains, thereby providing the evidence needed to timely optimize prevention and control strategies and measures across endemic regions. supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Friday, November 13, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Hantavirus Cases Highlight Climate-Driven Zoonotic Spillover Risks by November 10, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 5 mins read 0 Hantavirus Cases Highlight Climate-Driven Zoonotic Spillover Risks Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Recent reports of hantavirus-associated disease linked to cruise travel in South America have renewed international attention to the growing influence of climate and environmental change on zoonotic disease emergence. Although the World Health Organization currently assesses the public health risk associated with this specific event as low, the outbreak serves as a timely reminder that zoonotic spillover is increasingly shaped by ecological disruption, climate variability, and human mobility. While hantavirus disease remains concentrated in specific endemic regions, the ecological mechanisms underlying its transmission provide valuable insights into how climate and environmental change can influence zoonotic disease risks more broadly. This perspective, published in BMC Global and Public Health, argues that the recent event illustrates a critical shift in global health preparedness, moving from isolated biological events to complex socioecological challenges. The emergence and spread of zoonotic diseases have become defining challenges of the twenty-first century. Approximately 60% of emerging infectious diseases in humans are zoonotic in origin, and most arise from wildlife reservoirs. Historically, disease emergence was often viewed as an isolated biological event. However, growing evidence indicates that climate change, biodiversity loss, land-use change, agricultural expansion, and urbanisation are altering ecological systems in ways that facilitate pathogen transmission between animals and humans. These changes influence wildlife host dynamics, vector ecology, pathogen persistence, and human exposure, creating new opportunities for disease emergence and spread. The recent hantavirus event provides a timely example of this transition, illustrating how ecological disruption and global connectivity can intersect to amplify spillover opportunities and public health concerns. Importantly, such events highlight a critical weakness in current global preparedness systems: surveillance and response frameworks remain overwhelmingly reactive, focusing primarily on outbreak detection after human transmission has already occurred, rather than on anticipating ecological conditions associated with spillover emergence. As climate-related environmental change accelerates globally, understanding the ecological drivers of spillover is becoming increasingly important for global health preparedness. The occurrence of hantavirus cases within ecotourism and international travel networks demonstrates how localised ecological disturbances can be amplified by global mobility, turning a regional health issue into an international concern. This intersection of local ecology and global connectivity underscores the need for a more anticipatory approach to disease surveillance. Hantaviruses are rodent-borne pathogens maintained in wildlife reservoir species, particularly rodents within the Muridae and Cricetidae families. Human infection typically occurs through inhalation of aerosolised particles contaminated with rodent urine, saliva, or feces. Unlike directly transmitted respiratory pathogens, hantaviruses primarily represent environmentally mediated zoonotic spillover events occurring at the human–animal–environment interface. From an eco-epidemiological perspective, hantavirus transmission dynamics are tightly coupled to rodent population ecology. Climatic factors such as rainfall, temperature, humidity, and vegetation productivity strongly influence rodent abundance, breeding cycles, and habitat distribution. This coupling means that shifts in climate directly impact the likelihood of human exposure to the pathogen. Increased rainfall can promote vegetation growth and food availability, leading to rapid rodent population expansion, whereas drought conditions may drive rodents closer to human settlements. Both scenarios can increase opportunities for zoonotic transmission. Extreme weather events, including floods, droughts, and storms, may further alter host–pathogen interactions and increase spillover risk. As climate change intensifies the frequency and severity of such events globally, the ecological systems governing zoonotic spillover are becoming increasingly unstable and unpredictable. These dynamics extend well beyond hantaviruses. Climate-sensitive mechanisms are increasingly recognised across a broad range of infectious diseases. For example, dengue fever continues to expand geographically in response to changing temperature and rainfall patterns, while flooding events contribute to outbreaks of leptospirosis and other environmentally mediated diseases. The emergence of Japanese encephalitis virus in southeastern Australia since 2022 has further highlighted how environmental change, vector ecology, wildlife reservoirs, and animal hosts can converge to facilitate disease emergence. Recent outbreaks of Ebola virus disease in Africa and the COVID-19 pandemic have likewise demonstrated how localised spillover events can rapidly escalate into international public health emergencies. Together, these examples illustrate how environmental change, ecological disruption, and global connectivity are reshaping infectious disease risks across borders. Climate affects not only pathogen survival and vector biology, but also biodiversity, wildlife behaviour, ecosystem stability, and human exposure patterns. Emerging infectious diseases must therefore be understood not solely as biomedical phenomena, but as manifestations of increasingly unstable socioecological systems. At the same time, international travel and trade enable emerging infections to spread rapidly beyond their origins and become regional concerns. The COVID-19 pandemic further reinforced the consequences of failing to address ecological drivers of disease emergence. Although the origins of SARS-CoV-2 remain under investigation, the pandemic demonstrated how ecological disruption, wildlife interfaces, and global mobility can rapidly transform localised spillover events into global public health emergencies. This experience exposed significant limitations in existing preparedness systems, which remained largely reactive, focusing on outbreaks after human cases occur. Yet many zoonotic diseases are preceded by measurable environmental and ecological changes, highlighting the need to strengthen climate-informed surveillance systems capable of identifying elevated spillover risk before outbreaks emerge. The One Health framework provides an important foundation for addressing these challenges. By integrating human, animal, and environmental health surveillance, One Health can improve understanding of disease emergence and support earlier intervention. However, despite widespread policy support, operational implementation remains fragmented across many countries and institutions. The recent hantavirus event highlights the urgent need to strengthen climate-informed and ecologically informed surveillance systems. Future pandemic preparedness must move beyond reactive outbreak response toward anticipatory frameworks capable of identifying spillover risk before sustained human transmission occurs. Recent advances in remote sensing, artificial intelligence, environmental monitoring, climate forecasting, and predictive analytics provide new opportunities to operationalise this approach. Environmental indicators, including rainfall anomalies, vegetation change, temperature variability, and land-use patterns, may help identify ecological conditions associated with increased disease risk before widespread transmission occurs. An important future direction will be the development of integrated climate-informed early warning systems capable of linking environmental monitoring, ecological surveillance, wildlife reservoir dynamics, and human disease data in near real time. Such systems may help identify ecological conditions associated with elevated spillover risk, support spatial risk prediction, and enable earlier public health intervention before widespread transmission occurs. A conceptual framework for these systems outlines the integration of diverse data streams to create a cohesive early warning capability. Integrating climate, environmental, wildlife, vector, and human disease surveillance data within a One Health framework may improve early detection of zoonotic spillover risk. Such systems can support risk prediction, hotspot detection, early warning, and public health preparedness for climate-sensitive emerging infectious diseases. More broadly, climate change is no longer simply a contextual background factor for infectious diseases. Rather, it is increasingly reshaping the ecological systems governing reservoir host dynamics, vector ecology, pathogen maintenance, and human exposure patterns. As biodiversity loss, land-use change, and environmental disruption continue to intensify globally, the frequency and complexity of zoonotic spillover events are likely to increase. These challenges expose important limitations in predominantly reactive outbreak-response systems. Future preparedness will require more anticipatory and integrated approaches capable of linking climate science, environmental monitoring, wildlife surveillance, and public health systems within climate-informed One Health frameworks. Advances in remote sensing, predictive modelling, and environmental intelligence may provide important opportunities to strengthen early warning capacity and improve preparedness for climate-sensitive emerging infectious diseases. Ultimately, the recent hantavirus event should not be interpreted as an isolated outbreak, but as part of a broader planetary health challenge emerging from increasingly unstable interactions among climate, ecosystems, wildlife, and human societies. Strengthening climate-informed One Health approaches may therefore become one of the most important priorities for reducing future pandemic risk in a rapidly changing environmental future.
